etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English langage, language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from Old Latin dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”). Doublet of langaj. Displaced native Old English ġeþēode.

definitions.definition: (countable) A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form of communication.

quote.citation: 1867, Report on the Systems of Deaf-Mute Instruction pursued in Europe, quoted in 1983 in History of the College for the Deaf, 1857-1907 →ISBN, page 240:
quote.text: Hence the natural language of the mute is, in schools of this class, suppressed as soon and as far as possible, and its existence as a language, capable of being made the reliable and precise vehicle for the widest range of thought, is ignored.

quote.citation: 1900, William Beckford, The History of the Caliph Vathek, page 50:
quote.text: No language could express his rage and despair.

quote.citation: 2000, Geary Hobson, The Last of the Ofos, →ISBN, page 113:
quote.text: Mr. Darko, generally acknowledged to be the last surviving member of the Ofo Tribe, was also the last remaining speaker of the tribe's language.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The ability to communicate using words.

quote.citation: 1805 December, Julius Griffiths, “A Journey across the Desert”, in The Monthly Mirror, page 362:
quote.text: It is wholly out of the power of language to convey any idea of the blissful enjoyment of obtaining water, after an almost total want of it, during eight and forty hours, in the scorching regions of an Arabian desert, in the month of July.

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 15:
quote.text: Language is the articulation of the limited to express the unlimited; it is the ultimate mystery which is the image of God, for in breaking up infinity to create finite beings, God has found a way to let the limited being yet be a reflection of His unlimited Being.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A sublanguage: the slang of a particular community or jargon of a particular specialist field.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, “Prologue: Who is Edmund Gray?”, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Thus, when he drew up instructions in lawyer language, he expressed the important words by an initial, a medial, or a final consonant, and made scratches for all the words between; his clerks, however, understood him very well.

quote.citation: 1991 September, Stephen Fry, chapter 1, in The Liar, London: Heinemann, →ISBN, →OCLC, section II, page 24:
quote.text: And ‘blubbing’ . . . Blubbing went out with ‘decent’ and ‘ripping’. Mind you, not a bad new language to start up. 1920s schoolboy slang could be due for a revival.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable, figurative) The expression of thought (the communication of meaning) in a specified way; that which communicates something, as language does.

quote.citation: 2001, Eugene C. Kennedy, Sara C. Charles, On Becoming a Counselor, →ISBN:
quote.text: A tale about themselves [is] told by people with help from the universal languages of their eyes, their hands, and even their shirting feet.

quote.citation: 2005, Sean Dooley, The Big Twitch, Sydney: Allen and Unwin, page 231:
quote.text: Birding had become like that for me. It is a language that, once learnt, I have been unable to unlearn.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) A body of sounds, signs and/or signals by which animals communicate, and by which plants are sometimes also thought to communicate.

quote.text: A more likely hypothesis was that the attacked leaves were transmitting some airborne chemical signal to sound the alarm, rather like insects sending out warnings  […]  But this is the first time that a plant-to-plant language has been detected.
Prairie dogs use their language to refer to real dangers in the real world, so it definitely has meaning.

definitions.definition: (computing, countable) A computer language; a machine language.

quote.citation: 2015, Kent D. Lee, Foundations of Programming Languages, →ISBN, page 94:
quote.text: In fact pointers are called references in these languages to distinguish them from pointers in languages like C and C++.
Their language simple, as their manners meek,  […]

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The particular words used in a speech or a passage of text.

quote.text: "Where the hell is Horace?" ¶ "There he is. He's coming. You shouldn't use language."

definitions.definition: (rare, now nonstandard or technical) To communicate by language; to express in language.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: Others were languaged in such doubtful expressions that they have a double sense.

definitions.definition: An admonishment said in response to vulgar language.
A languet, a flat plate in or below the flue pipe of an organ.

quote.citation: 1896, William Horatio Clarke, The Organist's Retrospect, page 79:
quote.text: A flue-pipe is one in which the air passes through the throat, or flue, which is the narrow, longitudinal aperture between the lower lip and the tongue, or language.  […]  The language is adjusted by slightly elevating or depressing it,  […]
